citation.title: The Effect of Images of Michelle Obama's Face on Trick-or-Treaters' Dietary Choices: A Randomized Control Trial

standing_assumptions:
The paper is a six-page empirical report with no theorem, no displayed formula and no formal model; it states no potential-outcome notation and no identification assumption. The setting, as printed (read from the page images):
Abstract, Design (p. 1/6): "Multi-year randomized control trial." Intervention (p. 1/6): "Random assignment to the Michelle Obama side of the porch or the Comparison side of the porch." Main outcome measure (p. 1/6): "Selection of fruit over candy." Methods (p. 1/6): "Difference-in-means estimates."
Methods (pp. 2/6-3/6): "We ran the following versions of an experiment during Halloween trick-or-treating in 2012 (n = 165, on average 7.8 years old and 58% male), 2014 (n = 422, on average 8.5 years old and 56% male), and 2015 (n = 636, on average 8.7 years old and 49% male): children were randomly assigned to one of two sides of a porch (In 2012, random assignment was done via drawing pieces of paper from a brown bag; In 2014 and 2015 random assignment was a pseudo-random process via queuing order of children and the speed with which each side completed the last participant)."
Methods (p. 3/6): "One side of the porch–denoted Obama–had a large photo of Michelle Obama in front of the children. The other side–denoted Comparison–had a photo of Ann Romney (2012), a photo of Hillary Clinton (2014, 2015), or no photo (2014, 2015). (See S1 Table for the disaggregation of comparison groups.) Other posters were taped to the wall that said either “Obama” or “Romney”/“Clinton” on the respective sides of the porch. In 2014, we primed the trick-or-treater by pointing to the photo and asking if they knew who that was; in 2015, trick-or-treaters were individually randomly assigned (using a pre-coded Excel spreadsheet) to receive or not receive the additional priming. We pool our analysis, irrespective of this additional source of variation."
Outcome (p. 3/6): "At both sides of the porch, children were asked their age and whether they would prefer to receive fruit (a box of raisins) or candy (a more typical small packaged piece of name-brand chocolate such as Snickers or Milky Ways). Each child was given the option (fruit or candy) that they requested."
Analysis (pp. 3/6-4/6): "For analysis, we use the difference-in-means estimates for each year. (We had missing outcome data on one 12 year old, female participant in 2012; this participant is dropped from analysis. Our findings are substantively unchanged by imputing either a fruit or candy outcome for the participant.) To compute the pooled estimates, we aggregate across years using inverse probability of treatment weighting. For all estimates, we form Wald-type confidence intervals using a normal approximation-based estimation using heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors as calculated in R 3.2.3."
Not varied or measured in the study: exposure to the Let’s Move initiative, or any link between the porch condition and the initiative's health message (Introduction, p. 2/6: "an experimental evaluation of the effects of the entire campaign would not be possible due to the initiative being rolled out across the United States through mass media"). The targets below exist only because finding P035-E001 is rated Major and its validators gave an exact finite counterexample; none of the paper's headline claims is a mathematical statement.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, Conclusions, first sentence (the campaign attribution); the witness is the validators' construction and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: Abstract Conclusions, p. 2/6 (PDF p. 2), and Results and conclusions, p. 5/6 (PDF p. 5); the Introduction, p. 2/6, supplies hypothesis and rationale, not a separate categorical error
canonical_claim.statement:
Nonidentification witness for the campaign attribution (validator's construction; not in the paper). For each year $y \in \{2012, 2014, 2015\}$ let $(p_{y0}, p_{y1})$ be the released complete-case fruit frequencies in the pooled comparison arm and the Obama arm: $(14/69,\ 24/95)$, $(58/265,\ 37/157)$, $(113/444,\ 61/192)$. Let $L_y$ be the least common multiple of the two reduced denominators and $t_{yz} = L_y\,p_{yz}$, so that $(L_y, t_{y0}, t_{y1}) = (6555, 1330, 1656)$, $(41605, 9106, 9805)$, $(7104, 1808, 2257)$. Latent population: $R$ uniform on $\{1,\dots,L_y\}$. $Z \in \{0,1\}$ is assignment to the implemented Obama porch condition ($Z=1$) or its pooled comparison ($Z=0$), randomized independently of $R$ within year, with consistency and no interference granted. $A \in \{0,1\}$ is the presence ($A=1$) or absence ($A=0$) of the Let's Move initiative; the study takes place under $A=1$ throughout. Binary potential outcomes (1 = raisins, 0 = candy):
$$D_y(z,a;r)=\mathbf{1}\{r\le t_{y0}+z\,(t_{y1}-t_{y0})\}\quad\text{(direct-display world)},$$
$$C_y(z,a;r)=\mathbf{1}\{r\le t_{y0}+a\,z\,(t_{y1}-t_{y0})\}\quad\text{(campaign-enabled world)}.$$
Claims. (i) Observational equality in the observed setting: $C_y(z,1;r)=D_y(z,1;r)$ for every $y$, $z$ and $r$. (ii) Calibration to the six released year-by-arm frequencies: $\#\{r: D_y(z,1;r)=1\}/L_y = p_{yz}$ for $z=0,1$ and each $y$. (iii) Zero campaign effect for every child in $D$: $D_y(z,1;r)-D_y(z,0;r)=0$ for every $y$, $z$, $r$. (iv) Positive campaign effect in $C$ at the Obama condition: $C_y(0,1;r)-C_y(0,0;r)=0$ for every $r$, and $E[C_y(1,1;R)-C_y(1,0;R)]=(t_{y1}-t_{y0})/L_y = 326/6555,\ 699/41605,\ 449/7104$ for $y=2012, 2014, 2015$, each $>0$; with $P(\text{year}=y, Z=1)$ equal to the raw Obama shares $96/1223$, $157/1223$, $192/1223$, the mean campaign effect at the assigned condition, $E[C_y(Z,1;R)-C_y(Z,0;R)]$ taken over years and assignments, is $\tfrac{96}{1223}\tfrac{326}{6555}+\tfrac{157}{1223}\tfrac{699}{41605}+\tfrac{192}{1223}\tfrac{449}{7104}=\tfrac{83755728}{5240292055}>0$, against $0$ in $D$. (v) Consequence: $D$ and $C$ give the same outcome for every child under every assignment in the observed setting $A=1$, hence the same law of (year, $Z$, observed choice) for any assignment mechanism, yet different campaign effects; so the campaign effect is not a function of the observed law, and a real effect of the porch condition under valid randomization does not imply an effect of the initiative.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: From the paper: the Obama and Comparison sides of the porch (Methods, p. 3/6); the outcome, choice of fruit (a box of raisins) over candy (p. 3/6); years 2012, 2014, 2015 with n = 165, 422, 636 (pp. 2/6-3/6). From the released data, as extracted and asserted by the validators' scripts: enrolled / complete-case / fruit counts by year, comparison then Obama: 2012: 69/69/14 and 96/95/24; 2014: 265/265/58 and 157/157/37; 2015: 444/444/113 and 192/192/61 (one missing outcome, Obama side, 2012). Not in the paper and defined by the validator (P035-E001/v2/artifact/derivation.md, sections 2-4): the latent index R, the campaign indicator A (a policy counterfactual, not a measured exposure), the potential-outcome functions D and C, the campaign effect Y(z,1;r) - Y(z,0;r), and identification (two models with the same observed law must agree on the target).
canonical_claim.note:
The statement follows validator v2 (uniform R on {1..L}, integer thresholds), which needs no comparison sub-arm labels. Validator v1 gives an equivalent construction with rational atoms and comparator tags (P035-E001/v1/artifact/derivation.md sections 2-3, exact_models.json, check.py); its 2015 Clinton/no-photo split (55, 58) is one allocation compatible with S1 Table, not a recovered split, so it is not the version to formalize. All numbers above were recomputed in exact rational arithmetic when this list was fixed. The counts in (ii) and (iv) are cardinalities of initial segments, so no enumeration of the 55,264 latent values is needed. What a proof establishes: the inference from the porch-condition contrast to an effect of the initiative is invalid without further assumptions. What it does not establish: that the initiative had no effect; Sol records both falsity fields as null. The artifacts also contain a second pair of models (photo component against name display, v1 section 4, v2 section 5); it is not a target, because Sol did not refute the abstract's Results sentence under its natural reading as a label for the whole porch condition.

Accepted review: the categorical attribution under scrutiny is the abstract conclusion and the campaign-effect wording on p. 5/6. The Introduction explicitly discloses the implemented porch intervention, says that evaluation of the entire nationwide campaign is impossible, and offers campaign reinforcement as something that may occur. Its purpose and may-reinforce rationale are context, not separate categorical errors or required corrections. That rationale imposes neither an exclusion nor a bound on non-campaign pathways. The two exact observationally equivalent worlds establish nonidentification without refuting reinforcement as a possible explanation, deciding the real-world campaign effect, or altering the numerical porch-condition evidence. The Major finding is retained on this narrower basis.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, Conclusions, first sentence, and 'the treatment effect of her campaign' (p. 5/6), as repaired by Sol
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's corrected text (validated.json, P035-E001, prior_correction.corrected_text; the same repair as smallest_repair), verbatim: "These trials estimate that assignment to the implemented Michelle Obama porch condition increased the probability of choosing raisins rather than candy relative to the pooled comparison conditions. Campaign reinforcement is a possible explanation; the experiment does not establish that the initiative or its health message caused the difference. On p.5, describe the effect of the implemented Michelle Obama porch condition rather than the treatment effect of her campaign."
Mathematical content of the two clauses about the campaign, in the notation of P035-T1 (validator derivations, v1 section 3 and v2 sections 3-4): (a) "does not establish": among potential-outcome models with $Z$ randomized independently of the latent type, consistency and no interference, the campaign effect $E[Y(1,1;R)-Y(1,0;R)]$ is not determined by the law of (year, $Z$, observed choice) under $A=1$; that is, there exist two such models with the same observed law, equal to the six released year-by-arm frequencies $(14/69,\ 24/95)$, $(58/265,\ 37/157)$, $(113/444,\ 61/192)$, in one of which the campaign effect is $0$ for every child and in the other of which it is strictly positive in each year. (b) "a possible explanation": the second model reproduces the same six frequencies and attributes the whole porch-condition contrast $p_{y1}-p_{y0}$ $(=326/6555,\ 699/41605,\ 449/7104)$ in each year to the campaign.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: As for P035-T1. The printed sentences being replaced: Abstract, Conclusions, first sentence (p. 2/6) and "the treatment effect of her campaign" (Results and conclusions, p. 5/6); both are transcribed in P035-T3.
canonical_claim.note:
The first sentence of the corrected text keeps the paper's estimate unchanged and is an empirical estimate, not a theorem; whether the porch condition in fact raised raisin choice is not a Lean matter and depends on the assignment questions left undetermined in P035-N001 and P035-N002. Its arithmetic is exact and optional here: with enrolled counts $n_{yz}$, complete-case counts $m_{yz}$, fruit counts $k_{yz}$ and weights $w_{yz}=(n_{y0}+n_{y1})/n_{yz}$, the pooled means $\mu_z=\sum_y k_{yz}w_{yz}/\sum_y m_{yz}w_{yz}$ are $\mu_0=64881881/275804845$ and $\mu_1=1722050/6135717$, so $\mu_1-\mu_0=76852873088573/1692260476148865>0$ and $\mu_1/\mu_0-1=76852873088573/398096860243677$ (printed as 23.5%, 28.1% and 19%). The two means and their difference are already proved in Lean in the P035-N004 validator's artifact (P035-N004/v1/artifact/check.lean, theorems authorsMeans and differences), so they need not be redone. The standard error and p = 0.091 involve a square root and a normal tail and are not targets. Parts (a) and (b) are corollaries of P035-T1 and should reuse its definitions.

Accepted review: the categorical attribution under scrutiny is the abstract conclusion and the campaign-effect wording on p. 5/6. Its purpose and may-reinforce rationale are context, not separate categorical errors or required corrections. That rationale imposes neither an exclusion nor a bound on non-campaign pathways. The two exact observationally equivalent worlds establish nonidentification without refuting reinforcement as a possible explanation, deciding the real-world campaign effect, or altering the numerical porch-condition evidence. The Major finding is retained on this narrower basis.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Abstract, Conclusions (first sentence), with Abstract, Results
canonical_claim.location: Abstract Conclusions/Results, p. 2/6 (PDF p. 2), and campaign-effect wording in Results and conclusions, p. 5/6 (PDF p. 5); read with the Introduction's contextual hypothesis and rationale
canonical_claim.statement:
Abstract, Conclusions (p. 2/6): "Michelle Obama’s initiative to reduce childhood obesity has influenced children’s dietary preferences. Whether this influence extends beyond Halloween trick-or-treating in New Haven, CT on the porch of an economics professor requires further research."
The evidence it rests on, Abstract, Results (p. 2/6): "We estimate that viewing a photograph of Michelle Obama’s face relative to control conditions caused children to be 19% more likely to choose fruit over candy."
Contextual hypothesis and rationale, not a separate categorical attribution. Introduction (p. 2/6): "However, we have experimentally assessed the microfoundations of Let’s Move in order to evaluate whether the public health campaign altered dietary decision-making. When children are exposed to the image of a figurehead regularly associated with the public health campaign’s message, the subconscious reminder may reinforce the message." 
The separate campaign-effect wording. Results and conclusions (p. 5/6): "In particular, this is a strongly Democratic neighborhood, and if children in Democratic households are either more aware of Michelle Obama’s campaign or more favorably disposed to it, we would generate an overestimate of the treatment effect of her campaign on the general population of those in the United States."
Qualification the paper attaches (Introduction, p. 2/6): "While the campaign gained publicity, an experimental evaluation of the effects of the entire campaign would not be possible due to the initiative being rolled out across the United States through mass media."
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: "Michelle Obama’s initiative": the Let’s Move Initiative (Introduction, p. 2/6: "In 2010, Obama unveiled her Let’s Move Initiative, aimed at fostering a healthy lifestyle and reducing childhood obesity."). "Dietary preferences": observed as the choice of fruit (a box of raisins) or candy (Methods, p. 3/6). The Obama and Comparison conditions (Methods, p. 3/6). The pooled estimates (Results and conclusions, pp. 4/6-5/6): "28.1% (95% CI 23.8–32.4%) of participants in the Obama treatment select fruit instead of candy, in contrast to only 23.5% (20.5–26.5%) of participants in the pooled comparison group. The difference is statistically significant at the 0.10 level (two-sided p = 0.091)." The paper defines neither "influenced" nor any assumption linking the porch condition to the initiative.
canonical_claim.note:
Not a mathematical statement: an empirical causal attribution with no formal hypotheses, listed because finding P035-E001 (Major) touches it and the brief asks for the statement as printed. Its only formalizable content is the inference it draws, namely that every potential-outcome model consistent with the design (randomized porch assignment, consistency, no interference) and with the observed arm frequencies has a nonzero effect of the initiative. That rendering is this audit's reading for the purpose of the counterexample, not the paper's wording, and P035-T1 refutes it. Lean cannot decide whether the initiative in fact influenced these children. If nothing can be stated beyond the universal claim that P035-T1 already refutes, not_applicable is the right status. The brief's priority scale has no level for a printed statement that is not a mathematical headline result; 3 is used so that it comes after the counterexample and the corrected statement.

Accepted review: the categorical attribution under scrutiny is the abstract conclusion and the campaign-effect wording on p. 5/6. The two exact observationally equivalent worlds establish nonidentification without refuting reinforcement as a possible explanation, deciding the real-world campaign effect, or altering the numerical porch-condition evidence. The Major finding is retained on this narrower basis.
